strengths: The paper introduces a useful and timely resource: 992 articulated digital-twin assets across 9 categories and 37 subcategories, plus sim-ready indoor scenes, pixel-level affordance annotations, and modular interaction behaviors. This addresses a real bottleneck in robot learning simulation assets.

The focus on articulated objects with visual realism, physical tuning, USD format, and embedded reusable interaction semantics is practically valuable and goes beyond many existing asset collections that are static, visually weak, or simulator-specific.

The manuscript includes multiple forms of validation, including comparisons to PartNet-Mobility and BEHAVIOR-1K, optical motion-capture measurements for physical behavior, and downstream imitation-learning and reinforcement-learning experiments with real-world deployment.
The resource-oriented contribution is potentially high impact for embodied AI and robot learning if the assets, annotations, and production guidelines are fully released as claimed.
The paper is generally clear about the asset creation pipeline and gives useful appendix details on category counts, modeling time, annotation labels, physics equations, and learning hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The evaluation of visual realism is not fully convincing. Triangle count, qualitative renderings, and t-SNE visualizations of CLIP features are weak proxies for photorealism or sim-to-real usefulness, and there is no perceptual study or rigorous quantitative rendering-domain metric.

The physical-fidelity validation is narrow relative to the scale of the dataset. The main quantitative motion-capture evidence appears to cover only a small number of object types and mechanisms, so it is unclear how well the claimed fidelity generalizes across 992 assets and thousands of joints.

Downstream robot-learning experiments are promising but somewhat confounded. Mixed real-plus-sim data often uses more total data than real-only settings, so gains do not isolate asset quality from data quantity. The sim-only success rates are still substantially below real-only in several tasks.

Comparisons to existing datasets are partially unfair or incomplete. BEHAVIOR-1K and PartNet-Mobility differ in format, simulator integration, licensing/access constraints, and intended scope; the paper would benefit from stronger controlled baselines, including domain randomization and asset-quality ablations.

The modular interaction system is a central novelty, but its technical specification is underdeveloped. The paper describes behavior primitives but does not provide enough detail on APIs, portability outside Isaac Sim, failure modes, or how users author and compose new behaviors.

Reproducibility remains uncertain from the manuscript alone. The abstract says data are available but the shown URL is blank, and important details such as license terms, file organization, exact evaluation splits, asset-quality validation protocol, and code release status are not fully specified.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially broad claims that ArtVIP reduces the sim-to-real gap or provides high physical fidelity across the whole dataset. The evidence supports usefulness, but not yet the full generality implied by the framing.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck for robot learning: high-quality articulated digital assets with visual appearance, joint behavior, and simulation usability packaged together.

The proposed dataset appears substantially useful if released as claimed: 992 articulated objects, six sim-ready scenes, USD format, part/affordance annotations, and some reusable interaction primitives.

The manuscript includes several forms of validation beyond screenshots, including real-world imitation-learning tasks, a comparison to PartNet-Mobility on a microwave task, and optical motion-capture comparisons for selected joint motions.
weaknesses: The central claims of visual realism and physical fidelity are not convincingly established. Visual realism is supported largely by triangle counts, qualitative renderings, CLIP/t-SNE plots, and one reconstruction example, none of which provide a rigorous or perceptual measure of realism.

Physical fidelity evaluation is narrow relative to the dataset scale. A few selected objects/joints are compared to real-world trajectories, but the paper claims high physical fidelity across 992 assets and thousands of joints without systematic error statistics, coverage analysis, or failure cases.

The downstream robot-learning experiments are suggestive but confounded. Real-sim mixed training uses more total data than real-only training, so improvements do not cleanly isolate the value of simulation assets. The PartNet-Mobility comparison is limited to microwaves and does not control for many asset-level differences.

The paper is primarily a manually authored dataset/resource contribution, with limited technical novelty. The joint-drive modifications and modular interactions are described at a high level and seem mostly engineering decisions within Isaac Sim rather than a general algorithmic contribution.

Reproducibility is a major concern. The abstract has an apparently blank data URL, and the manuscript does not provide enough detail to verify licensing, asset availability, generation/tuning procedures, or whether all claimed resources will be accessible in practice.

Several claims are overstated. For example, the Pearson correlation between simulation and real-world RL checkpoints is based on very few points and does not by itself demonstrate simulator fidelity. Similarly, t-SNE alignment of CLIP features is not strong evidence of sim-to-real usefulness.

The comparisons to prior datasets are sometimes dismissive and not always fair: BEHAVIOR-1K is evaluated through a different framework/version, and categorical labels such as visual realism high/medium/low and physical fidelity high/low are asserted without objective scoring criteria.

Writing and presentation issues reduce confidence: there are typos, formatting problems, duplicated/awkward phrasing, unclear equations, and some tables/figures that are hard to interpret from the provided text.

strengths: The paper introduces a valuable articulated-object asset dataset with 992 digital-twin assets across 9 categories and 37 subcategories, plus scenes, pixel-level annotations, joint metadata, and modular interaction behaviors. This is a meaningful resource contribution for robot learning.
weaknesses: The evidence for visual realism is somewhat indirect. Triangle counts, qualitative renderings, reconstruction examples, and t-SNE/CLIP visualizations are suggestive, but they do not fully establish photorealism or task-relevant visual fidelity compared with stronger perceptual metrics, user studies, or broader downstream perception evaluations.
